Ajahn, what is the central practice of 'Reflective Contemplation' in Dhammapada Reflections Volume 1?

In Volume 1 of Dhammapada Reflections, Ajahn Munindo emphasizes that contemplation (yoniso manasikāra) is the art of holding sacred verses in the heart until they illuminate our daily blind spots.

You don't read the verse like a novel; you read a single verse, close your eyes, and allow the truth to penetrate your current emotional reactivity. It transforms ancient verses into living, personal medicine.

In your daily life, cultivate the grounded stillness of The One Who Knows (Buddho). Do not push away difficult experiences with aversion, and do not cling to pleasant sensations with craving. See all changing mental and physical states as impermanent, conditioned phenomena (anicca saṅkhāra) that are empty of an enduring self (anattā). By resting in silent, spacious awareness, your heart abides in the unshakable peace of the Unconditioned (Asaṅkhata Dhamma).

Ajahn, how do we practice with the Dhammapada verse on 'He Abused Me, He Struck Me'?

The verse says: ''He abused me, he defeated me, he robbed me'—in those who harbor such thoughts, hatred will never cease.'

Ajahn Munindo explains that carrying old grievances is like picking up a red-hot coal with the intention of throwing it at someone else—you are the one who gets burned! When you drop the repetitive narrative of victimhood, the burning coal is discarded, and your heart is liberated into peace.

Ajahn, what is the practice of 'The Island of Self-Reliance' in Volume 1?

The Buddha urged: 'Make an island of yourself, make yourself your refuge; there is no other refuge.'

In a world of fluctuating economies, broken relationships, and uncertainty, external things cannot provide absolute security. By cultivating inner virtue, mindfulness, and wisdom, you construct an indestructible island of Dhamma within your own heart that no tsunami of worldly change can ever wash away.

Ajahn, how does Ajahn Munindo explain 'The Art of Not Interfering' in meditation?

'The Art of Not Interfering' is allowing phenomena to arise, play out, and dissolve in awareness without jumping in to fix, adjust, or control them.

We interfere out of anxiety: wanting good thoughts to stay and bad thoughts to leave. But when you step back and act as the silent, impartial witness, the natural self-cleansing power of consciousness is activated, leading to effortless samādhi.

Ajahn, what is the practice of 'The Gentle Touch' in handling difficult emotions in Volume 1?

When difficult emotions arise—grief, shame, or loneliness—do not attack them with harsh spiritual judgment.

Apply 'The Gentle Touch': hold the hurting emotion in the vast, warm embrace of unconditional compassion (mettā), just as a loving mother holds a feverish child. In that gentle warmth, the frozen trauma dissolves.

Ajahn, what is the practice of 'Returning to the Source' in Volume 1?

Returning to the source means stepping back from external distractions into the silent wellspring of pure awareness within.

Whenever the mind feels scattered or overwhelmed by worldly tasks, take three conscious breaths and rest in 'Buddho.' In that quiet return, your spiritual energy is instantly renewed.

Ajahn, how does Volume 1 guide us to overcome self-judgment in meditation?

Self-judgment is a toxic defilement that attacks the mind when meditation does not meet our high expectations.

Replace self-judgment with **Yoniso Manasikāra (wise reflection)**: Recognize that restlessness or sleepiness are simply natural conditions arising from causes. Meet the struggle with gentle kindness, adjust the effort, and continue practicing with patience.

Ajahn, what is the final blessing of Dhammapada Reflections Volume 1?

May the wisdom of the Dhammapada illuminate your mind in every situation.

May you be protected from all harm, freed from all defilements, and established in the supreme peace of Nibbāna!

**Sādhu! Sādhu! Sādhu!**

Ajahn, how do we practice with 'Since ancient times it has been the case' in Dhammapada Reflections Volume One?

It is natural to encounter challenges when contemplating since ancient times it has been the case. In *Dhammapada Reflections Volume One*, the teaching guides us to bring direct, non-judgmental mindfulness (sati) to this very moment. Notice the felt sense in the body and the subtle movements of the heart (citta) as you investigate: observe the arising and passing away of thoughts without claiming ownership. When we recognize that all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāras) are impermanent (anicca) and not-self (anattā), the grip of craving (taṇhā) naturally loosens. It is like a traveler resting beneath the shade of a great forest banyan tree: you enjoy the cool shelter without trying to carry the tree on your back. Anchor your mind in peaceful knowing presence (Buddho), and let reality unfold with wisdom.
